options.C: Inability to focus on one single duty
options.D: Multi-skilling and clinical versatility

explanation: Spot on! Being able to switch tasks across different units proves you have great clinical versatility and multi-skilling abilities.

question: A student nurse accidentally pricks a finger with a used injection needle. What is the very first thing to do?

options.A: Suck the puncture site vigorously to extract infected blood
options.B: Cover the wound with adhesive plaster and finish the shift
options.C: Wash the wound thoroughly with soap and running water
options.D: Apply a tight tourniquet above the elbow to trap the virus

explanation: Spot on! Immediate washing with soap and running water helps wash away germs right after an exposure. Always remember this rule!

question: A nurse is getting a patient ready for a pacemaker insertion. What is the very first thing that must be done?

options.A: Shave the entire chest wall from nipple to neck
options.B: Program the pacemaker to a high heart rate
options.C: Administer the post-procedure antibiotics early
options.D: Verify that the informed consent form is signed

explanation: Making sure the patient understands the procedure and signs the consent form always comes first before any physical preparation begins. Well done!

question: Which brain structure acts as the main relay station for sorting incoming sensory information?

options.A: Hypothalamus
options.B: Thalamus
options.C: Medulla oblongata
options.D: Cerebellum

explanation: The thalamus filters and relays sensory signals up to the correct regions of the cerebral cortex. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T3#GNS211_U3_T3_h4)

question: What is the name of the thick, yellowish milk produced in the first few days after birth?

options.A: Foremilk
options.B: Colostrum
options.C: Hindmilk
options.D: Transition milk

explanation: Colostrum is the first milk produced after birth, packed with high concentrations of protective antibodies for the newborn. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T015#GNS226_U3_T015_h3)

question: Which of these best describes a quality improvement framework in action?

options.A: Punishing staff members immediately whenever a patient complains about waiting times
options.B: Collecting clinic data to identify service gaps and testing small changes to fix them
options.C: Hiding poor treatment outcomes from hospital management to avoid criticism
options.D: Stopping all routine data collection until the end of the calendar year

explanation: You got it! Quality improvement is all about looking at data, spotting problems, and testing little tweaks to see what makes patient care better. [learn more](GNS312_U5_T2#GNS312_U5_T2_h7)

question: Which part of the brain matures last during the teenage years, affecting self-control?

options.A: Limbic system
options.B: Cerebellum
options.C: Brainstem
options.D: Prefrontal cortex

explanation: You nailed it! The prefrontal cortex is our brain's planning and decision-making center, and it's one of the last areas to fully mature.

question: In many resource-limited settings, how do most patients pay for their hospital care?

options.A: By exchanging farm produce for treatments
options.B: Through free international donor grants
options.C: Through direct out-of-pocket spending
options.D: Using universal government health insurance

explanation: That's right! Without widespread health insurance, most people pay for their care straight from their own pockets when illness strikes.

question: What happens to a pregnant woman's resting heart rate?

options.A: It fluctuates wildly every hour
options.B: It decreases significantly below baseline
options.C: It increases by 10 to 15 beats per minute
options.D: It remains completely unchanged

explanation: Correct! The heart beats a bit faster to pump the extra blood needed during gestation. You're doing great!

question: How can a nurse tell the difference between normal pregnancy breathlessness and a serious lung issue?

options.A: Serious lung problems disappear completely as soon as the patient drinks water
options.B: Normal dyspnoea lacks warning signs like chest pain, coughing blood, or low oxygen levels
options.C: Normal dyspnoea causes blue lips and severe finger clubbing
options.D: Normal dyspnoea only occurs when the patient is lying flat on her back

explanation: Ordinary shortness of breath feels safe and stable, but red flags like chest pain or low oxygen mean we must investigate right away.

question: A nurse picks up a sterile surgical tray from the supply room and notices the outer paper wrapper is damp. What should she do?

options.A: Dry the outside wrapper carefully with a clean towel and use it
options.B: Check the chemical indicator strip and use the tray if the color changed
options.C: Consider the item contaminated and return it for re-sterilization
options.D: Open the package immediately before the moisture spreads further

explanation: Moisture on packaging acts like a sponge, pulling bacteria right through the barrier. It's best to safely reprocess it!

question: Which glove material gives you a great feel (tactile sensitivity) but can cause nasty allergies?

options.A: Nitrile
options.B: Neoprene
options.C: Vinyl
options.D: Latex

explanation: Natural rubber latex fits like a second skin, but protein allergies make it a risk for both healthcare workers and patients.

question: What type of energy do infrared thermometers pick up from the human body?

options.A: Sound wave echoes
options.B: Electrical current
options.C: Ultraviolet radiation
options.D: Infrared radiation

explanation: These thermometers are built to sense the invisible heat energy that naturally radiates from warm human skin.

question: What is the main goal of using aseptic technique in the ward?

options.A: To prevent pathogen contamination during clinical procedures
options.B: To cure patients who already have active bacterial infections
options.C: To completely eliminate all microbes from the hospital environment
options.D: To reduce the financial cost of hospital-acquired illnesses

explanation: You've got this! Aseptic techniques are just safe practices we use to stop harmful germs from getting into clean or sterile parts of the body during procedures. Keep it up!

question: A community nurse notices a sudden spike in typhoid cases in a village. What is the best first move?

options.A: Close all schools in the country permanently
options.B: Order immediate quarantine for every healthy person in the region
options.C: Stop all routine vaccinations until the investigation ends
options.D: Investigate potential sources like local water supplies and food handlers

explanation: To stop an outbreak, you have to play detective! Tracking down contaminated water or food handlers helps you find the exact source.

question: Which counselling approach features the clinician taking a strong, expert role to give direct instructions?

options.A: Non-directive counselling
options.B: Peer support counselling
options.C: Community outreach counselling
options.D: Directive counselling

explanation: In directive counselling, the clinician provides clear, firm guidance and instructions on what the patient must do. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T002#GNS227_U7_T002_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a good way to prevent medication errors?

options.A: Minimizing hallway conversations while calculating doses
options.B: Double-checking high-alert calculations with a colleague
options.C: Carefully reading medication labels three separate times
options.D: Rushing through drug rounds to finish ahead of schedule

question: Why do we always send a written referral form when moving a patient from a primary clinic to a big teaching hospital?

options.A: It ensures continuity of care and prevents miscommunication between facilities
options.B: It legally transfers hospital ownership of the patient's medical history
options.C: It guarantees that the receiving doctor will provide free treatment
options.D: It allows the patient to bypass hospital registration queues entirely

explanation: Great job thinking like a nurse! Writing things down carries the patient's vital clinical details across, so the receiving team instantly knows what care has already been given.

question: What is the most life-threatening type of bleeding that can happen to someone with a severe bleeding disorder?

options.A: Intracranial hemorrhage
options.B: Epistaxis from the nose
options.C: Petechiae on the skin
options.D: Gingival bleeding while brushing

explanation: Bleeding inside the skull (intracranial hemorrhage) puts heavy pressure on the brain. It can cause rapid confusion, unconsciousness, or worse if nurses don't catch it early.

question: Which nursing care helps stop joint stiffness in an unconscious patient?

options.A: Frequent administration of diuretics
options.B: Passive range-of-motion exercises
options.C: Keeping the patient flat on the back
options.D: Applying warm compresses to the chest

explanation: Spot on! Gently moving their arms and legs through their normal motion keeps the joints flexible while they can't move on their own.

question: Why is patient confidentiality harder to maintain in home health care?

options.A: Electronic health records are broadcasted on public radio channels
options.B: Family members and visitors are often present during private medical discussions
options.C: Private homes have glass walls that block all soundproofing
options.D: Nurses are required by law to publish treatment notes in local newspapers

explanation: The open nature of a household makes it difficult to keep clinical conversations and health details completely private. [learn more](GNS324_U1_T11#GNS324_U1_T11_h7)

question: What is the main goal of the whole operating theatre team?

options.A: Ensuring safe and coordinated patient care during surgery
options.B: Training new medical students in advanced surgical skills
options.C: Cleaning and disinfecting the theatre after every procedure
options.D: Maintaining hospital financial records and surgical supplies

explanation: Great job thinking about teamwork! Everyone in the theatre works hand-in-hand to keep the patient safe and make sure the surgery goes smoothly. You've got this!

question: During drug breakdown, what actually happens in a chemical process called hydrolysis?

options.A: Hydrogen atoms are removed to increase drug activity
options.B: A chemical bond is split by adding a water molecule
options.C: A bulky chemical group is attached to block kidney filtration
options.D: Oxygen is added to the drug molecule directly from the air

question: What is the biggest downside of keeping a patient on a clear fluid diet for too long?

options.A: It provides excessive amounts of complex carbohydrates.
options.B: It contains an unsafe amount of dietary fiber and roughage.
options.C: It lacks adequate calories, protein, and essential nutrients.
options.D: It causes immediate permanent weight gain in most patients.

explanation: Clear fluids are mostly water and sugar. They are great for a quick rest, but they won't give the body the building blocks it needs to heal long-term.

question: What is the main role of the thalamus when processing sensory information?

options.A: Act as a relay station to filter and direct signals to the cortex
options.B: Store long-term memories of painful experiences
options.C: Control the physical movement of the sensory organs
options.D: Convert mechanical waves into electrical nerve impulses

explanation: Think of the thalamus as the ultimate sorting office in the brain. It checks incoming sensory messages and routes them to the right neighborhood in the cortex for you to experience them.

question: What is the main job of red bone marrow?

options.A: Synthesizing the organic collagen matrix
options.B: Producing blood cells through hematopoiesis
options.C: Storing energy reserves as triglycerides
options.D: Releasing calcium ions directly into bone

explanation: Red marrow is our body's busy factory for making red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Excellent!

question: What is a major benefit of starting breastfeeding within the first hour of life?

options.A: It helps the baby receive nutrient-rich colostrum and stimulates uterine contraction
options.B: It prevents the mother from experiencing postpartum hair loss
options.C: It replaces the need for any future childhood vaccinations
options.D: It completely guarantees that the child will never catch malaria

explanation: You got it! Early breastfeeding gives baby immune-boosting colostrum and helps mum's uterus contract naturally.

question: Which needle gauge is best for a routine subcutaneous injection?

options.A: 32 to 36 gauge
options.B: 20 to 22 gauge
options.C: 25 to 30 gauge
options.D: 14 to 18 gauge

explanation: Higher gauge numbers mean thinner needles! A 25 to 30 gauge needle slips in smoothly and keeps the injection as painless as possible.

question: Why is it important for a nurse to recognize the physical and psychological signs of early or forced marriage?

options.A: To report the patient to international news agencies for public awareness
options.B: To prescribe financial aid directly from the hospital pharmacy fund
options.C: To automatically discharge the patient without further medical evaluation
options.D: To provide targeted clinical care, appropriate counseling, and safe referrals

explanation: Great job! Recognizing these signs helps nurses deliver specialized medical care, emotional support, and safe links to protective social services.

question: Why do doctors often check kidney function labs before putting a patient on long-term NSAID therapy?

options.A: To determine how fast the liver breaks down the medicine
options.B: To make sure the kidneys can handle the drug without failing
options.C: To calculate the exact blood sugar level of the patient
options.D: To check if the patient has a hidden urinary tract infection

explanation: Checking baseline creatinine and BUN ensures the kidneys are tough enough to handle the slight dip in blood flow that NSAIDs can cause. Smart nursing assessment! [learn more](GNS223_U5_T4#GNS223_U5_T4_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of presenting data in nursing research?

options.A: To make raw information easy to understand and use
options.B: To replace the need for written conclusions
options.C: To make research articles longer and more academic
options.D: To hide errors in clinical measurements

explanation: Presenting data organizes chaotic raw information into a clear format so readers can easily grasp clinical findings. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T6#GNS217_U4_T6_h1)

question: Why might a patient show signs of a delayed transfusion reaction a few days after getting blood?

options.A: The patient forgot to take prescribed post-transfusion antibiotics
options.B: Low-level antibodies increased over time and attacked newly introduced cells
options.C: The blood bag was stored in a refrigerator that was too cold
options.D: The intravenous cannula was left in place for too many days

explanation: Sometimes antibodies are so low in number that lab tests miss them initially. Once exposed to the donor cells, those antibody levels rise and start a delayed attack.

question: Wernicke encephalopathy is caused by a severe shortage of which vitamin?

options.A: Vitamin D
options.B: Vitamin B12
options.C: Vitamin C
options.D: Vitamin B1

explanation: Spot on! Wernicke encephalopathy happens specifically when the body lacks enough thiamine, which is Vitamin B1.

question: What key detail does a drug label tell you about its strength?

options.A: The amount of active drug per tablet, capsule, or milliliter
options.B: The name of the drug rep
options.C: The patient's diagnosis
options.D: How much the hospital paid for it

explanation: The label strength tells you the concentration—how much medicine is actually packed into each pill or mL.

question: Why do nurses take a detailed health history when assessing a patient's blood (haematological) health?

options.A: To calculate the exact financial cost of patient care
options.B: To catch subtle clues about blood and clotting abnormalities
options.C: To diagnose the exact type of cancer immediately
options.D: To replace the need for routine laboratory blood tests

explanation: Spotting early clues in a patient's history helps you catch blood and clotting issues before they become serious. Great job thinking like a nurse!

question: What is the main goal of a street drop-in center?

options.A: To provide immediate basic needs like food, water, and first aid
options.B: To train children exclusively in advanced computer programming
options.C: To lock up troubled youths until they agree to pay fines
options.D: To serve as a permanent lifelong housing facility

explanation: Spot on! Drop-in centers are safe havens where kids can grab a meal, get medical care, and feel welcomed.

question: How do traditional African belief systems generally view the role of food in daily life?

options.A: As a purely chemical fuel source with no cultural significance
options.B: As items that should only be consumed alone in silence
options.C: As a sacred gift tied to ancestry, community, and spiritual balance
options.D: As a dangerous substance that must be minimized through fasting

explanation: In these rich traditions, food is much more than fuel—it connects the living to their ancestors, their community, and spiritual wellness.

question: Under normal circumstances, how often should you check cervical dilation during active labour?

options.A: Once every 24 hours
options.B: Every 30 minutes
options.C: Every 4 hours
options.D: Every 15 seconds

explanation: Checking every 4 hours gives you a clear picture of how labour is advancing while keeping the risk of infection low.

question: What is the difference between abdominal bloating and abdominal distension?

options.A: Bloating is a feeling of fullness, while distension is visible swelling of the abdomen.
options.B: Bloating only occurs in the stomach, while distension only occurs in the rectum.
options.C: Distension is caused by swallowed air, whereas bloating is caused by poor hygiene.
options.D: Bloating causes sharp pain, while distension is completely painless.

explanation: Bloating is how the patient *feels* (internal pressure), while distension is what you can actually *see* (a swollen tummy). Easy distinction!

question: A post-op patient presses a handheld button on their IV machine to release a safe dose of pain meds. What is this device called?

options.A: Enteral feeding pump
options.B: Large Volume Pump
options.C: Insulin ambulatory pump
options.D: Patient-Controlled Analgesia pump

question: What is the main job of wearable health devices in clinical care?

options.A: To deliver oral medications automatically to the patient
options.B: To diagnose complex surgical diseases without a doctor
options.C: To track and transmit health-related data continuously
options.D: To replace traditional laboratory blood testing completely

explanation: Wearables are great because they keep an eye on patient vitals between clinic visits. You've got this!

question: Why might a patient scheduled for bariatric (weight loss) surgery be put on a low-calorie diet beforehand?

options.A: Building up large leg muscle stores
options.B: Shrinking liver size to ease surgery
options.C: Preventing all post-operative pain
options.D: Accelerating skin wound healing time

explanation: Exactly! Diets low in calories help reduce fat and glycogen stored in the liver, making it smaller and giving the surgeon a much clearer view during the operation.

question: Why do pelvic tissues need several weeks to bounce back after delivery?

options.A: Complete recovery happens instantly once the placenta is expelled
options.B: Breastfeeding prevents any healing from occurring in the lower body
options.C: The uterus remains heavy for at least a full year
options.D: Hormones must normalize and stretched muscle fibers need time to repair

explanation: That's right! Healing takes time—hormones need to settle down while overworked muscle fibers patiently rebuild themselves.

question: What severe long-term complication can happen when a baby's head presses against soft tissues for too long during obstructed labour?

options.A: Hyperemesis gravidarum
options.B: Pregnancy-induced hypertension
options.C: Obstetric fistula
options.D: Gestational diabetes

question: A patient suddenly feels a strong need to pee and leaks a little before reaching the toilet. What is this called?

options.A: Urinary incontinence
options.B: Hematuria
options.C: Renal failure
options.D: Urinary retention

question: What makes a patient outcome goal measurable in a care plan?

options.A: It includes specific criteria like pain scores or timeline targets
options.B: It is written only by the attending physician
options.C: It states that the patient will feel better eventually
options.D: It relies entirely on the nurse's personal opinion

explanation: You got it! Measurable goals use clear indicators—like a specific pain scale number or a timeframe—so you can easily tell if the patient is improving.

question: Why is home delivery not recommended as a default option for every pregnant woman?

options.A: Government policies ban home births completely
options.B: Hospitals prefer to keep all pregnant women admitted
options.C: Unforeseen complications can arise suddenly during labor
options.D: Traditional birth attendants charge too much money

explanation: Labor can become unpredictable very quickly, making facility care necessary for women who develop unexpected risks. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T9#GNS225_U3_T9_h1)

question: What is the main purpose of doing regular mental health checks on these patients?

options.A: To prove that the family is doing a poor job at home
options.B: To test the patient's physical strength and walking balance
options.C: To find a permanent cure for the underlying genetic mutation
options.D: To catch subtle shifts in mood and thinking early and guide care

explanation: Spot on! Catching small mental changes early helps nurses update safety plans and support systems before things get overwhelming. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T13#GNS222_U4_T13_h4)

question: What should you do if a patient cannot speak because they have an endotracheal breathing tube in their throat?

options.A: Score the patient with a verbal score of 1 for total silence
options.B: Give the patient a verbal score of 5 assuming they are normal
options.C: Document the verbal score as untestable and note the breathing tube
options.D: Leave the verbal score section completely blank on the chart

explanation: Never guess! When a physical barrier like a breathing tube stops you from testing, clearly document why you couldn't check it so other nurses understand.

question: How does palliative care view the dying process?

options.A: As a medical failure that must be avoided
options.B: As a punishment for past misdeeds
options.C: As a condition that can always be reversed
options.D: As a normal and natural part of life

explanation: Palliative care philosophy regards dying as a normal human process that neither hastens nor postpones death. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T1#GNS321_U4_T1_h2)

question: What is the most immediate danger when someone has severe, nonstop vomiting and diarrhea?

options.A: Upper airway obstruction
options.B: Chronic hair loss
options.C: Severe dehydration
options.D: Permanent hearing impairment

explanation: Losing water and electrolytes too fast causes blood pressure to crash, which can quickly become life-threatening if not treated.

question: Why is obstructed labor more common among very young mothers?

options.A: Cephalopelvic disproportion caused by an immature pelvis
options.B: Premature hardening of the fetal cranial bones
options.C: Excessive physical exercise during the third trimester
options.D: Over-consumption of dietary iron during the first trimester

explanation: Spot on! Because a young girl's pelvis is still growing, it might be too small for the baby's head to pass through easily.

question: What is the primary cause of varicose veins?

options.A: Atherosclerotic plaque blocking deep arteries
options.B: Too many red blood cells being made in the bone marrow
options.C: Sudden arterial spasm from cold weather
options.D: Damaged or weak valves inside the veins

explanation: When vein valves get tired or damaged, they can't close properly. Blood pools in the lower legs, stretching the veins out into those bumpy, twisted varicose lines.

question: Which parasite is responsible for causing ascariasis?

options.A: Necator americanus
options.B: Ascaris lumbricoides
options.C: Enterobius vermicularis
options.D: Schistosoma haematobium

explanation: Ascariasis is caused by Ascaris lumbricoides, commonly known as the giant roundworm. You'll see this often in community health postings!

question: How does the 'revolving' part of a DRF actually work in practice?

options.A: Unsold expired drugs are returned to manufacturers for full cash refunds
options.B: Donors inject new capital into the pharmacy every single month
options.C: Money collected from drug sales is used to buy fresh stock
options.D: Profits from drug sales are returned to the government treasury

explanation: Spot on! Patients buy drugs, that money goes back into the kitty, and the pharmacy uses it to buy the next batch. It is a continuous loop that keeps the pharmacy stocked.

question: When is a doctor or lab scientist most likely to order a peripheral blood smear along with a regular full blood count?

options.A: As a quick kidney check before surgery
options.B: To check how much iron the patient eats over time
options.C: When the standard blood count shows unexpected results
options.D: To replace measuring total haemoglobin

explanation: A blood smear lets the lab actually look at the cells under a microscope when the numbers on the regular blood test look a bit strange.

question: What is a major social barrier that prevents Nigerian teenagers from seeking care?

options.A: Fear of community gossip and moral judgment from adults
options.B: Excessive availability of youth-only private hospitals everywhere
options.C: Mandatory free transport provided by local government councils
options.D: Strict laws requiring teenagers to study nursing in secondary school

explanation: Cultural stigma and the fear of being judged or gossiped about in the community stop many young people from visiting clinics. [learn more](GNS312_U4_T4#GNS312_U4_T4_h3)

question: What makes probability sampling special?

options.A: Every member of the population has a known chance of being selected
options.B: The researcher hand-picks individuals who fit a specific profile
options.C: Only patients with severe symptoms are included in the study
options.D: Participants are chosen based on their easy availability to the nurse

explanation: Spot on! Probability sampling uses fairness and random selection, meaning everyone in the group has a fair shot at being chosen.

question: In public health, what do we mean by an epidemiological 'agent'?

options.A: The primary factor that must be present for a disease to occur
options.B: The vector that carries a microbe from place to place
options.C: The immune response produced by a healthy host
options.D: The physical environment where a patient lives

explanation: Think of the agent as the root cause or spark—like a bacterium or virus—without which the disease simply cannot happen. You've got this!

question: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the clinic with chronic anxiety, low self-esteem, and frequent physical complaints with no clear organic cause. What background factor should the nurse suspect?

options.A: Standard adolescent adjustment issues to high school
options.B: Trauma and isolation from an early forced marriage
options.C: Immediate physical recovery from a sports injury
options.D: Mild seasonal affective disorder

explanation: Young brides experience intense psychological pressure, social isolation, and loss of control, manifesting as chronic anxiety and somatic complaints. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T14#GNS312_U1_T14_h3)

question: What is the best move when a nurse is giving diet advice to a patient with a tight budget?

options.A: Handing them a strict shopping list of expensive imported supplements
options.B: Focusing only on rare medical terms without explaining the food items
options.C: Telling them to completely stop eating all traditional carbohydrate staples
options.D: Suggesting affordable local food substitutions that fit the patient's budget

explanation: Brilliant! Good nursing care meets patients where they are financially, offering realistic, pocket-friendly local food options.

question: Why do blood disorders like sickle cell anaemia often cause deep emotional distress for patients?

options.A: Because of the unpredictable pain crises and lifelong nature of the illness
options.B: Because daily physical therapy is strictly mandatory for everyone
options.C: Because patients get a quick and complete cure in most hospitals
options.D: Because there are never any physical symptoms during early stages

explanation: Living with a chronic condition that flares up unexpectedly takes a heavy mental toll. Understanding this helps you support the whole patient, not just their labs!

question: What is the main feature of a non-experimental research design?

options.A: The researcher does not manipulate any variables
options.B: Data is collected exclusively through open-ended interviews
options.C: The study takes place inside a controlled laboratory
options.D: Participants are randomly assigned to treatment groups

explanation: In non-experimental studies, you simply observe and measure things as they naturally are without stepping in to change them.

question: What is the primary cause of occupational lung diseases?

options.A: Smoking cigarettes without using a proper filter
options.B: Breathing in harmful workplace dusts and chemicals
options.C: Severe bacterial infections caught in the community
options.D: Inherited genetic defects of the respiratory tract

explanation: These conditions are directly caused by inhaling hazardous substances present in the work environment over a long period. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h1)

question: Where are muscarinic receptors mostly found in the human body?

options.A: The brainstem exclusively
options.B: Smooth muscle and glands
options.C: Skeletal muscle only
options.D: Spinal nerve roots

explanation: Correct! Muscarinic receptors hang out on effector organs like smooth muscle, heart muscle, and various glands.

question: Why is it best to look up medications by their generic name in the formulary?

options.A: It prevents confusion because one drug can have many different brand names
options.B: It stops patients from experiencing any side effects
options.C: It ensures the medication is always available free of charge
options.D: It proves that the drug was manufactured locally in Nigeria

explanation: A single drug can have dozens of brand names, but the generic name is always the same everywhere in the world!

question: Why are bedside nurses considered central to hospital quality assurance?

options.A: They are responsible for hospital budget approvals
options.B: They spend the most time directly caring for patients
options.C: They write all the medical textbooks in the country
options.D: They alone have the power to hire new doctors

explanation: You know it! Because you are right there at the bedside 24/7, you are in the best position to catch safety gaps and make care better.

question: What is the main job of antibiotics in our bodies?

options.A: To treat and manage bacterial infections
options.B: To boost overall red blood cell counts
options.C: To replace lost fluids and electrolytes
options.D: To lower elevated body temperature rapidly

explanation: You got this! Antibiotics are specifically made to hunt down and stop bacteria from causing trouble in the body. They don't touch viruses or fever on their own!

question: What is the main job of the hypothalamus when you experience stress?

options.A: Slowing down your heart rate so you can fall asleep
options.B: Filtering visual signals coming from your eyes
options.C: Linking emotional triggers to physical stress and hormone responses
options.D: Storing facts you learned during your nursing lectures

explanation: You got it! The hypothalamus connects emotional feelings from the limbic system to physical body changes by triggering hormones and your nervous system.

question: Which type of glaucoma happens suddenly and comes with severe pain because the drainage angle is completely blocked?

options.A: Angle-closure glaucoma
options.B: Secondary pigmentary glaucoma
options.C: Open-angle glaucoma
options.D: Normal-tension glaucoma

explanation: That's right! In angle-closure glaucoma, the iris suddenly blocks the drainage path, trapping fluid and causing a painful, emergency spike in eye pressure.

question: Why should we involve parents and community leaders in adolescent health programs?

options.A: To shift cultural norms and build supportive safety nets for teens
options.B: To give adults total control over adolescent personal decisions
options.C: To ensure healthcare facilities collect more financial profit
options.D: To eliminate the need for professional nursing staff

explanation: Correct! When community leaders and parents are on board, stigma drops and teenagers find a safer network to ask for help.

question: An antibiotic costs 500 Naira to land in the pharmacy, and hospital policy adds a 20 percent mark-up. What is the retail price?

options.A: 520 Naira
options.B: 550 Naira
options.C: 600 Naira
options.D: 700 Naira

explanation: Let's do the quick math: 20 percent of 500 Naira is 100 Naira. Add that mark-up to the original 500 Naira cost, and you get a final retail price of 600 Naira. Easy peasy!

question: How does a well-motivated nurse protect patient safety at the bedside?

options.A: By removing the need for doctors to write formal medication orders
options.B: By automatically doubling the nurse-to-patient staffing ratio
options.C: By increasing vigilance to catch subtle signs of clinical deterioration early
options.D: By speeding up the discharge process regardless of clinical status

explanation: When you are alert and motivated, you easily notice tiny changes in a patient's condition and can save the day early!

question: A nurse checks a patient's pedal pulses and finds the left pulse is strong while the right pulse cannot be felt at all. What is the most immediate clinical concern?

options.A: High blood pressure throughout the body
options.B: A potential blockage in the right leg artery
options.C: An allergic reaction to heart medication
options.D: A normal variation in elderly patients

explanation: An absent pulse on only one side strongly suggests local arterial occlusion or injury, requiring urgent follow-up. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T2#GNS213_U1_T2_h4)

question: How does educating girls and women directly improve maternal health in a community?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need for hospitals and clinics
options.B: It empowers women to recognize pregnancy danger signs and seek prompt medical care
options.C: It guarantees that every woman will become a qualified midwife
options.D: It prevents women from ever getting pregnant

explanation: Education is powerful! When women understand health risks, they can spot danger early and make smart choices for themselves and their babies. [learn more](GNS216_U1_T6#GNS216_U1_T6_h3)

question: A community health nurse notices many young people in her village developing untreated high blood pressure. What action best reflects modern primary health care nursing practice?

options.A: Waiting inside the urban teaching hospital for patients to travel and find her
options.B: Focusing solely on childhood immunizations and ignoring adult health entirely
options.C: Organizing a local screening camp combined with lifestyle and diet counseling
options.D: Telling the villagers that chronic illnesses cannot be managed at the local level

explanation: Proactive community screening and health education bring prevention and early management directly to the people, fulfilling PHC goals. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T2#GNS124_U1_T2_h7)

question: Why is it important for nurses to understand healthcare laws?

options.A: To avoid personal liability and protect patient rights in clinical settings
options.B: To replace hospital lawyers during lawsuits
options.C: To prescribe medications independently when doctors are absent
options.D: To bypass getting consent from family members in emergencies

explanation: You got it! Knowing your legal boundaries helps you deliver safe care while keeping your license and patients protected.

question: What is a crucial piece of advice a nurse should give a patient starting daily hormone pills?

options.A: Double your dose whenever you feel stressed or tired
options.B: Never stop taking the medication without consulting your doctor
options.C: Stop the pills once your blood test results return to normal
options.D: Take the medication only when you feel sluggish or dizzy

explanation: Stopping hormone replacement out of nowhere can trigger a life-threatening crisis. Always remind patients to talk to their doctor first!

question: Why is a flatus tube generally left in place for only a short period, such as 20 to 30 minutes?

options.A: To ensure the tube does not dissolve inside the bowel
options.B: To prevent the kidneys from stopping urine output
options.C: To prevent pressure damage to the delicate rectal lining
options.D: To stop the patient from drinking too much water

explanation: Prolonged pressure from an indwelling tube can compromise blood flow to the rectal mucosa, leading to irritation, ulceration, or necrosis. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h5)

question: What is the main medication given during Active Management of the Third Stage of Labour (AMTSL)?

options.A: Ergometrine alone
options.B: Calcium gluconate
options.C: Oxytocin
options.D: Magnesium sulfate

explanation: You've got this! Oxytocin is our go-to medication because it works fast to help the womb contract safely after delivery.

question: What is the main reason for investigating a medication error on the ward?

options.A: To identify system and workflow issues that caused the mistake
options.B: To reduce the amount of documentation nurses must complete
options.C: To prove to patients that mistakes never happen in the hospital
options.D: To find a single staff member to blame and punish publicly

explanation: Well done! Modern nursing looks at errors as broken processes to fix, rather than just blaming individuals. That's how we build safer hospitals!

question: What is a very common early sign that patients with developing disseminated sclerosis report?

options.A: Complete paralysis of both legs
options.B: Vision changes like optic neuritis
options.C: Severe high blood pressure
options.D: Total loss of long-term memory

explanation: Keep an eye out for this: inflammation of the optic nerve causing blurry vision or eye pain is frequently one of the very first warning signs of MS.

question: Why is uncovering hidden health needs an important goal of community diagnosis?

options.A: Doctors refuse to treat patients who walk into the clinic
options.B: Hospital records always contain complete and flawless data
options.C: Many sick people stay at home and never visit a health facility
options.D: Government officials order nurses to hide serious diseases

explanation: Hospital registries only capture those who manage to reach the clinic, leaving out vulnerable people suffering in silence at home. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T3#GNS124_U3_T3_h2)

question: What is the main job of GnRH agonist medications when treating endometriosis?

options.A: To dissolve existing pelvic scar tissue and adhesions
options.B: To stimulate rapid ovulation and increase fertility chances
options.C: To permanently increase the secretion of progesterone from the adrenal glands
options.D: To suppress estrogen production and shrink endometrial implants

explanation: These drugs put the body into a temporary 'pause' state by blocking estrogen. Without estrogen fueling them, the misplaced tissue patches shrink away.

question: Why might you still need to watch a patient with a normal blood pressure for poor circulation?

options.A: Blood pressure is the least important vital sign in critical care
options.B: Blood pressure can remain normal even when tissue perfusion is failing
options.C: Blood pressure monitors are always inaccurate in the ICU setting
options.D: Normal blood pressure guarantees the heart is pumping perfectly

explanation: The body is smart—it can tighten blood vessels to keep numbers looking normal for a while, even when tissues are starving for oxygen.

question: A family caregiver feels super guilty just for wanting a single day off. What does this most likely point to?

options.A: The caregiver has completely abandoned the patient
options.B: The patient needs immediate admission to an intensive care unit
options.C: The caregiver is experiencing normal caregiver burnout and emotional strain
options.D: The caregiver is showing signs of physical infection

explanation: Caring for someone takes a massive emotional toll. Feeling guilty for needing a breather is a classic sign of burnout—remember to care for the caregivers too!

question: What goes wrong if you crush an extended-release capsule before giving it to a patient?

options.A: The medication will take twice as long to work
options.B: The entire dose is released at once, risking toxicity
options.C: The patient will experience no therapeutic effect
options.D: The active ingredients are completely destroyed

explanation: Crushing destroys the special timed-release design. Instead of a steady, safe trickle of medicine over hours, the patient gets a dangerous flood all at once!

question: Which federal law requires healthcare facilities to inform patients about advance directives upon admission?

options.A: The Patient Self-Determination Act
options.B: The Nursing Practice Act
options.C: The Health Insurance Portability Act
options.D: The Affordable Care Act

explanation: Passed in 1991, the Patient Self-Determination Act ensures that patients are told about their right to make advance directives when entering a healthcare facility. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T7#GNS221_U4_T7_h2)

question: When should nutritional screening typically happen for a newly admitted hospital patient?

options.A: Right before the patient is discharged home
options.B: At the final weekly multidisciplinary meeting
options.C: Only after the patient requests a meal tray
options.D: Within twenty-four hours of admission

explanation: Early screening within the first day helps catch risks before the patient's condition deteriorates. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h4)
